The East–West schism

History and saints · Church history

The East–West schism

4 sectionsNot completed
Notes

The East–West schism concerns a division between Eastern and Western Christian churches. These sources introduce two different parts of that history: political rivalry and disagreement about the Holy Spirit. St. Philaret’s catechism states the Orthodox position on procession, the term used here for the Spirit’s eternal relation to the Father.[1][2][3]

Political rivalry and church division[1]

The OCA history identifies rivalry between the Holy Roman Empire and the Byzantine Empire as something that intensified the division. This brief excerpt supplies a political factor; the complete chapter provides its wider historical setting.[1]

Read original passage

OCA: The Great Schism

And the rivalry between the Holy Roman Empire in the West and the Byzantine Empire in the East exacerbated the rift.

What does the Creed say about the Holy Spirit?[2]

St. Philaret grounds the wording that the Spirit proceeds from the Father in John 15:26. He argues that this wording, received in the Creed, should not be supplemented. He also distinguishes calling the Spirit the Spirit of the Son from saying that the Spirit proceeds from the Son. These are statements about the theological meaning of the Creed.[2]

Read original passage

Philaret: the procession of the Holy Spirit

241. Whence know we that the Holy Ghost proceedeth from the Father?

This we know from the following words of Jesus Christ himself: But when the Comforter is come, whom I will send unto you from the Father, even the Spirit of truth, which proceedeth from the Father, he shall testify of me. John xv. 26.

242. Does the doctrine of the procession of the Holy Ghost from the Father admit of any change or supplement?

No. First, because the Orthodox Church, in this doctrine, repeats the very words of Jesus Christ; and his words, without doubt, are an exact and perfect expression of the truth. Secondly, because the second œcumenical Council, whose chief object was to establish the true doctrine respecting the Holy Ghost, has without doubt sufficiently set forth the same in the Creed; and the Catholic Church has acknowledged this so decidedly, that the third œcumenical Council in its seventh canon forbade the composition of any new Creed.

For this cause John Damascene writes: Of the Holy Ghost, we both say that he is from the Father, and call him the Spirit of the Father; while we nowise say that he is from the Son, but only call him the Spirit of the Son. (Theol. lib. i. c. 11; v. 4.)

The linked chapter is the fuller OCA account of the Great Schism. It supplies the context surrounding the short political observation reproduced in this lesson.[1]
